problem: Prior communicative agents are trained by self-play with a fixed partner and single-round games, so speakers cannot adapt on the fly to novel partners with different language abilities. Neural RSA speakers are fixed after training and do not condition on the listener's past behavior.
motivation: Humans talk to many partners and adapt within short conversations by modeling the partner's mental state (theory of mind). The paper defines few-shot language coordination and asks whether a speaker that quickly infers a listener's ability can pick more effective and concise instructions.
key_idea: Meta-learn (MAML) a theory-of-mind model that predicts a listener's next action from the listener's interaction history, and use it to rerank the speaker's candidate instructions by predicted probability of the correct action, with a length cost.
insight: Explicitly modeling the listener with fast adaptation beats non-adaptive pragmatics: in the referential game the ToM speaker reaches 58.19% versus 42.83% for RSA and 37.38% for non-ToM. Prediction accuracy of the ToM model rises within a session, showing it adapts to individual listeners. Ablations show robustness to model size and inner steps (55.28-58.25%), while RSA with a single listener (39.32%) does much worse, showing the gain comes from population-level meta-learning and adaptation rather than reranking alone.
method: Population of listeners: neural listeners with identical architecture trained on different datasets; in the referential game, vocabularies are drawn from a Dirichlet over 10 languages, and in ALFWorld, instruction-level distributions are drawn per task type from Dirichlet distributions.
Multi-round asymmetric games: a speaker sees the goal and the listener does not; a session has N games and memory is kept across games, which creates pressure to adapt.
ToM model: same architecture as the listener; the mental state is its parameters, adapted from the support set of past (observation, message, action) triples.

MAML meta-learning: inner loop takes N_inner=5 gradient steps on the listener's history (inner lr 0.01, outer lr 1e-4), and the outer loop minimizes action-prediction NLL over sampled listeners and support-set sizes.

Instruction selection: pick the candidate m maximizing P_ToM(gold action | o, m, history)·exp(-κC(m)); training samples from this distribution mixed with a uniform one (σ=0.5) in a DAgger-like data aggregation.
Candidate pools: beam search producing 5 instructions in each of 10 languages (referential game), or 4 rule-based instructions per abstraction level (ALFWorld), with cost C(m)=2^i.
Theory: if the ToM model is ε-optimal and the candidate pool is good enough, the induced instruction distribution's KL to the optimal one is bounded.

setting.backbone: ResNet + LSTM ToM model (MAML meta-trained); speaker and listeners are ResNet+LSTM in the referential game and the ALFWorld listener model in navigation
setting.training_data: Referential game: 30k MSCOCO image-caption pairs translated into 9 languages, giving 120 listeners (80/20/20 train/val/test). ALFWorld: 50 listeners (30/10/10) trained on rule-based four-level instructions from expert trajectories.
setting.observation: Referential game: target and 9 distractor images (ResNet features) plus text messages; ALFWorld: text-based environment observations plus instructions
setting.action_space: Referential game: choose 1 of 10 images; ALFWorld: discrete natural-language commands (text actions)
setting.simulator: ALFWorld (built on ALFRED); MSCOCO referential game
setting.privileged: Speaker is given the goal and expert (gold) actions/trajectories to plan; the listener cannot see the goal.

numbers_note: Not a standard VLN benchmark. Referential game success rates are in Table 1 and the appendix table (non-ToM 37.38, RSA 42.83, ToM 58.19, gold 91.20). ALFWorld results appear only as a figure (game points vs. instruction length), so no numeric values are available.
results: In the multilingual referential game, the ToM-assisted speaker achieves 58.19% average success versus 42.83% for the RSA speaker and 37.38% for the non-ToM speaker (gold-standard 91.20%). In ALFWorld navigation, ToM speakers get higher game points at lower instruction cost than random speakers for κ in {0,1,2}, but not for κ=10.
limitations: Only tested on synthetic listener populations in a referential game and a rule-based-instruction ALFWorld, with no human partners.
Speaker candidate pools come from rule-based or pretrained speakers, so quality is capped by the pool and the cost function is only lightly explored.
Only first-order modeling; recursive belief modeling and the listener-side perspective are left for future work.
builds_on: Machine Theory of Mind (Rabinowitz et al. 2018)
